concepts.title: Algorithmic Fairness
concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic Fairness is the study of algorithm performance across different people and cultures to address and mitigate biases.
concepts.content: The field of Algorithmic Fairness studies the performance and fairness of algorithms across people, groups, and cultures. It seeks to address algorithmic biases and to develop strategies to ensure that computer vision algorithms don't reflect or create biases against different groups of people or cultures.
concepts.motivation_md: As computer vision systems are deployed in society, it is critical to ensure they do not produce discriminatory outcomes or perform poorly for specific demographic groups.
concepts.recap_md: - This field focuses on identifying and mitigating biases in algorithmic performance across diverse groups.

concepts.title: Demographic Bias in Facial Analysis
concepts.one_liner: Facial analysis systems often exhibit significant performance variations and false positive rates across different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race.
concepts.content: Facial detection asks whether there is a face in some image region, while facial analysis refers to measuring additional attributes of the face, including pose and identity. It is important to characterize the performance of facial analysis systems across demographic groups. A large Face Recognition Vendor Test by NIST examined the accuracy of face recognition algorithms for different demographic groups defined by sex, age, and race or country of birth. For one dataset, they found false positive rates were highest in West and East African and East Asian people, and lowest in Eastern European individuals. For many systems, this effect was large, with differences of up to a factor of 100 in recognition false positive rates between different countries of birth. However, more accurate systems showed less bias, and some supplied identification algorithms where false positive differentials were undetectable. It is critical to report both false negative and false positive rates for each demographic group to understand the biases of any facial analysis system in use.
concepts.motivation_md: Facial recognition is used in high-stakes scenarios like law enforcement and security; understanding demographic bias is essential to prevent systemic discrimination and improve system reliability.
concepts.recap_md: - Facial analysis accuracy can vary by a factor of 100 across different demographic groups.

concepts.title: Dataset Biases
concepts.one_liner: Algorithmic bias often stems from training datasets that represent only a narrow slice of the world, frequently favoring Western or high-income households.
concepts.content:
One cause of algorithmic bias can be a bias in the contents of the training dataset. Any dataset represents only one slice of the possible images and labels that one could capture from the world. Furthermore, the samples taken may be influenced by the background of the researchers gathering the dataset. For example, object recognition systems often perform much better for images from first-world households than for those from lower-income or non-Western regions, possibly due to better representation of high-income imagery in training sets.

(see figure: Images of household items, and their recognized classes by five object recognition systems @DeVries2019. The systems tend to perform worse for non-Western countries and for lower-income households...) 

As shown in (see figure: ...), systems tend to perform worse for household items from non-Western countries and lower-income households.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models are only as good as their data; if training sets lack diversity, the resulting models will fail to generalize to global populations and diverse socioeconomic contexts.
concepts.recap_md: - Datasets often reflect the socioeconomic and geographic biases of their creators.

concepts.title: GAN-based Dataset Debiasing
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can mitigate dataset bias by synthetically producing balanced image sets with controlled variations in protected attributes.
concepts.content:
One way to mitigate a biased dataset is to synthetically produce the images needed to provide the necessary balance or coverage. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can operate on a dataset to generate sets of images similar to those of the dataset, but differing from each other in controlled ways, such as changes in the apparent gender, age, or race of depicted people. 

One approach, Fairness GAN, includes a classifier trained to perform as poorly as possible on predicting a protected attribute, such as skin tone, while maintaining accuracy on a target label like attractiveness. Another approach uses GANs to generate pairs of realistic images that are balanced with respect to protected attributes to remove unwanted correlations. For example, if "wearing hat" is correlated with "wearing glasses" in the data, the GAN can augment the dataset with paired examples of people wearing hats both with and without glasses. A third approach injects constraints to require that model predictions follow the distributions observed within training data, assuming that data has the desired distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: Collecting perfectly balanced real-world data is often impossible; GANs provide a way to 'fill in the gaps' synthetically, ensuring models learn target features without relying on biased correlations.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs can generate synthetic data to balance representation of protected attributes like race or age.

concepts.title: Counterfactual Analysis with Transects
concepts.one_liner: Counterfactual transects use GANs to modify a single face variable at a time, allowing researchers to isolate and assess specific algorithmic biases.
concepts.content:
It may be difficult to distinguish whether a given biased result is caused by algorithmic bias or by biases in the testing dataset. One way to disentangle those is through experimentation: modifying variables of a probe image and examining the algorithm's decision. GAN models, coupled with human labeling to learn directions in the latent space corresponding to changes in desired attributes, allow for such experimental intervention. These counterfactual studies can lead to different conclusions than observational studies, which are often influenced by biased correlations in the testing dataset. Researchers use transects—paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable is modified—to provide a clean assessment of bias related to that specific variable.

(see figure: A GAN creates sequences of faces, called **transects**, where only one attribute changes @Balakrishnan2020)
concepts.motivation_md: Observational testing cannot prove why a model is biased; counterfactual analysis allows for controlled experiments to pinpoint exactly which attributes trigger biased model behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Transects are paths in a GAN's latent space that vary exactly one attribute while keeping others constant.

key_passage.text: paths through the GAN's latent space where only one face variable is modified. The variation in an algorithm's classification results along the images of the transect provides a clean assessment of any bias related to the variable being modified.

prereq.rationale: Understanding how datasets can be biased is fundamental to understanding the broader concept of algorithmic fairness.
GAN-based debiasing is a technique specifically designed to mitigate the issues caused by biased training datasets.
Counterfactual transects rely on the generative capabilities of GANs, which are introduced in the context of dataset debiasing.
Counterfactual transects are used to determine if biased results in facial analysis are caused by the algorithm itself or the underlying dataset.

overlay.rationale: Facial analysis performance gaps across demographics serve as a primary real-world illustration of algorithmic fairness challenges.
Dataset bias is introduced as a primary cause for the demographic disparities seen in facial analysis.
